newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to tighten control on alcohol sale, output.
newsitem.headline: Russia to tighten control on alcohol sale, output.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin has signed a decree tightening controls on ethyl spirit and alcohol production and sales, the president's press service said.

The decree, signed late on Wednesday before the start of a four-day national holiday, restricts the sale of beverages with an alcohol content over 12 percent to retail outlets with a walk-in sales space after July 1.
Street kiosks, which currently sell a wide range of alcoholic beverages, some of them of dubious origin and quality, would be banned from trade in vodka and other hard liquors.

The decree also recommends regional authorities to issue licenses to small distillers and wholesalers (less than 0.2 million liters of pure alcohol a year) in consultation with the Federal Service for Control of the State Alcohol Monopoly.
Currently small entrepreneurs are licensed by regional authorities while big players are licensed by the Federal Service, according to the service's head, Viktor Berestovoi.
Licencees would be included on a state register and only licenced and registered producers and wholesalers would be able to buy special tax stamps.
The order also calls for the government to draw up requirements for equipment to measure alcohol production at factories and a timetable for fitting the equipment.
The decree is the latest volley in a continuing campaign to bring order and increase state control over Russia's chaotic -- and highly lucrative -- alcohol market.
Desperate for revenue-boosting measures to plug a huge budget deficit hole, the Russian government is trying to raise funds by tightening its grip on liquor imports and domestic alcohol production.

The Soviet government used to receive up to one-third of its overall revenues from sales of vodka, but this share has fallen to only two percent in recent years while the domestic vodka industry is working at about 30 percent capacity.
